title: Mary Magdalene in the garden (John 20:1–18)
hook: she thinks he's the gardener until he says her name

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday, the silent day, when the Church says he went down to free the dead. Your line was god is in the silence too. What came up in your hour of quiet? Day sixty-eight. It's morning.

A name is a strange thing. A stranger reads it off a list and it's just a word. Someone who knows you says it once, quietly, across a crowded room, and it lands differently. Hold on to that. Early on the first day of the week, while it's still dark, Mary Magdalene walks to the tomb. The stone has been rolled away. The body is gone. She runs for Peter, they come and look and go home, and she stays outside the tomb, crying. Today: what happens to the one who stayed.
screen: `A NAME, SAID BY SOMEONE WHO KNOWS YOU.` → `STILL DARK. THE STONE MOVED.` → `SHE STAYS, CRYING.`

segments.voice: She bends to look into the tomb and sees two angels, who ask why she's weeping. They've taken my Lord away, she says, and I don't know where they've laid him. She turns around, and there's a man standing there. In the Douay-Rheims he asks: "Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?" She thinks he's the gardener. Sir, she says, if you've moved him, tell me where, and I'll take him. And then he says one word. "Mary." That's all. Not a proof. Not a speech. Her name. And she knows him. She turns and says: "Rabboni," which John explains means Master, my teacher. Notice the Gospel's honesty. She doesn't recognize the risen Jesus by his face. She knows him by the way he says her name. Then he sends her. Go to my brothers, he says, and tell them. And she goes to the disciples and says: "I have seen the Lord." In John's Gospel she is the first to see him risen, and she is sent to tell the ones who will tell everyone else. The Church calls her the apostle to the apostles, and in 2016 Pope Francis raised her day, 22 July, to a feast, like the apostles' own. One more thing to clear up. Later preaching called her a repentant prostitute. The Gospels never say that. It came from sermons, Pope Gregory the Great's among them, that blended her with other women in the Gospels, and the Church's calendar separated them again in 1969.
screen: `SHE THINKS HE'S THE GARDENER.` · `ONE WORD: MARY.` · `KNOWN BY HER NAME, NOT HIS FACE.` · `APOSTLE TO THE APOSTLES.` · then, large: `I HAVE SEEN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for your own name. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind the people who say your name the way it's meant to be said: a grandparent, a friend, someone who has known you for years. Hear it in their voice, once. Notice what happens as you hear it. Christians believe God knows each person by name, like that. If you pray, you can sit quietly and imagine your name said with that kind of love. The bell holds the time.
Rabboni. What Mary Magdalene called Jesus the moment she heard him say her name outside the empty tomb.
Your line: he says your name. Today, use people's names: the barista, the coworker, the person on the phone. Say them like they matter. Day sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of Mary Magdalene at the tomb on Easter Sunday morning, and keep her feast on 22 July as the apostle to the apostles.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mary Magdalene was the sinful woman who washed his feet.
what it means: she is the first witness of the risen Jesus in John, recognized him when he said her name, and was sent to tell the apostles.
what a scholar hears: the prostitute story comes from a sixth-century sermon of Gregory the Great blending several women. the calendar separated them in 1969, and in 2016 her day became a feast.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 20:15, 16 and 18 given from memory; confirm.
John 20:2–10: Mary runs to Peter and the other disciple, who see the tomb and go home; summarized in the hook.

Pope Francis raised the memorial of Mary Magdalene (22 July) to a feast by a decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship dated 3 June 2016; the title 'apostle of the apostles' goes back at least to Thomas Aquinas and Rabanus Maurus. Confirm.
The conflation with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and Mary of Bethany is traced to Gregory the Great's homily 33 (591); the 1969 General Roman Calendar revision separated them. Confirm.
'Christians believe God knows each person by name' draws on Isaiah 43:1 and John 10:3; not quoted.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what their head does in a crowd; 'the first witness of the resurrection' narrowed to what John says (the first to see him risen in John); cut 'has long called' and 'for centuries'; the Gregory the Great conflation is now taught here only (removed from day 59) and the 1969 calendar is now cited; practice no longer opens 'Think of' or tells the listener what happens in their chest.
